title: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
summary: How DiskANN serves a billion vectors from one SSD with a Vamana graph, alpha pruning and beam search, how FreshDiskANN handles updates, and how CAGRA builds and searches fixed-degree graphs on GPUs.
outcomes: Explain why in-memory graph indexes stop scaling and what an SSD-resident index must minimize
Run Vamana's RobustPrune by hand and predict how alpha changes the edges kept
Estimate SSD reads and round trips per query from beam width W and list size L
Describe how FreshDiskANN applies deletes and inserts without rebuilding the index
Trace CAGRA's rank-based pruning and one GPU search iteration, and choose between DiskANN, CAGRA and HNSW

lessons.title: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes

blocks.md: In the prerequisite course you saw HNSW: a proximity graph that greedy search walks toward the query, touching only a tiny fraction of the vectors. HNSW assumes the whole graph and every full-precision vector sit in RAM. That assumption is what breaks first when the dataset grows to a billion points.

Do the arithmetic for $N = 10^9$ vectors of 128 dimensions. Stored as float32 they take $10^9 \times 128 \times 4$ bytes = 512 GB. A graph with 64 neighbor ids per node, 4 bytes each, adds another 256 GB. A single workstation with 64 GB of RAM cannot hold either one. The bars below compute these footprints and compare them with 32-byte product-quantization (PQ) codes, which you met in the PQ course.

scenes.caption: An in-memory graph index needs the full vectors plus the adjacency lists: 512 + 256 = 768 GB for float32 data with 64 neighbors per node.
PQ with 32 bytes per vector shrinks the vectors to 32 GB, which fits in 64 GB of RAM. Everything else has to live somewhere cheaper.
DiskANN's split: only the 32 GB of PQ codes stay in RAM; full vectors and the graph (768 GB) go to an SSD, which costs far less per byte than DRAM.

blocks.md:
Before DiskANN there were two standard ways to cope, and the DiskANN paper (Subramanya et al., NeurIPS 2019) explains why both hurt:

- **Inverted index plus compression** (IVF with PQ, as in FAISS): small enough for one machine, but the lossy codes cap accuracy. The paper reports 1-recall@1 around 0.5 for such billion-scale indexes.
- **Sharding in-memory graphs**: high recall, but many machines. The paper cites a deployment splitting 2 billion vectors into 32 shards on 32 machines.

Why not just put the graph on an SSD? A retail SSD needs a few hundred microseconds per random read and serves roughly 300K random reads per second. Greedy search reads one node, waits, then decides the next node. The paper states the goal precisely: a few dozen random reads per query and fewer than ten round trips to the disk, preferably five. Naively moving an in-memory index to SSD costs several hundred reads per query.

Two numbers drive an SSD-resident index: **total reads per query** (limits throughput, since the SSD has a fixed IOPS budget) and **round trips per query** (limits latency, since each trip costs a few hundred microseconds). DiskANN attacks both: a graph with short search paths, and a search that issues several reads per round trip.

scenes.caption: The RAM side holds only compressed PQ codes plus an optional cache of nodes near the start node. The SSD holds one fixed-size record per node.
Search compares the query to PQ codes in RAM to decide which nodes to fetch, then reads those nodes' records (neighbor lists) from the SSD.
Each SSD record also holds the node's full-precision vector, so the final top candidates are re-ranked with exact distances at no extra I/O.

blocks.md: GPUs push in the other direction. They have high memory bandwidth and thousands of threads, but graph search is sequential and branchy. **CAGRA** (Ootomo et al., ICDE 2024, from NVIDIA) redesigns both the graph and the search so a GPU can build and search it fast. The plot lets you check footprints yourself for other sizes.

scenes.caption: Default: 128-d float32, R = 64, 32-byte PQ. At one billion points the full vectors need 512 GB, the graph 256 GB, the PQ codes 32 GB.
With 96-d vectors and R = 32 the full data still exceeds 64 GB of RAM long before a billion points, while PQ codes stay small.

blocks.question: A team stores a 1-billion-point, 128-d float32 graph index on SSD and searches it with plain greedy search, one node read per step. Queries take 300 node visits. What is the main problem?
options: The SSD runs out of capacity
Hundreds of sequential round trips, each a few hundred microseconds, push latency far beyond a few milliseconds
PQ codes do not fit in RAM
Greedy search cannot run on data stored on disk
blocks.explain: 300 sequential reads at a few hundred microseconds each is tens of milliseconds or more. DiskANN's paper targets a few dozen reads and fewer than ten round trips. Capacity is fine (768 GB fits on SSD), and 32 GB of PQ codes fit in 64 GB of RAM.

blocks.question: Why does DiskANN keep PQ codes for every point in RAM instead of reading vectors from the SSD to compute distances during the search?
options: Each neighbor's distance would then cost its own random read, multiplying I/O by the degree
PQ distances are exact
The SSD cannot store full vectors
RAM is cheaper than SSD
blocks.explain: Search must score every neighbor of every expanded node, which is dozens of distance computations per hop. Fetching each neighbor's vector from SSD would be a random read per neighbor. Approximate PQ distances in RAM steer the search; exact vectors are only needed for the nodes actually read.

lessons.title: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob

blocks.md: Vamana is the graph DiskANN builds. Like HNSW and NSG it is made of two routines: **GreedySearch**$(s, x_q, k, L)$, a best-first walk from a start node $s$ that keeps a list of the $L$ closest nodes seen, and **RobustPrune**$(p, \mathcal{V}, \alpha, R)$, which picks at most $R$ out-neighbors for node $p$ from a candidate set $\mathcal{V}$. The new ingredient is the parameter $\alpha \ge 1$.

RobustPrune works greedily. Take the candidate $p^*$ closest to $p$ and add the edge $p \to p^*$. Then delete from the candidate set every $p'$ that $p^*$ already covers, meaning a search sitting at $p^*$ is clearly closer to $p'$ than a search sitting at $p$. Repeat until the candidates run out or $p$ has $R$ edges. The covering test is:

blocks.tex: \text{remove } p' \text{ if } \alpha \cdot d(p^*, p') \le d(p, p')
blocks.caption: With alpha = 1 this is the sparse neighborhood graph (SNG) rule, a relative of the RNG, which HNSW and NSG use implicitly. With alpha > 1 a candidate is removed only if p* is closer to it by a factor of alpha.

blocks.md: A toy example on a 2D grid. Node **p** sits at (5, 4); six candidates A to F surround it. Coordinates are the grid positions in the figure, and every distance below is Euclidean, computed by script. Distances from p: B 1.41, D 3.00, C 4.47, F 5.00, A 5.10, E 5.39.

blocks.prompt: Run RobustPrune for p with alpha = 1 and no degree limit. B is picked first. Which of A, C, E, F does B cover? Then guess: will raising alpha to 1.2 add or remove edges?
blocks.reveal:
With alpha = 1, B covers A (4.00 vs 5.10), C (3.16 vs 4.47) and E (5.00 vs 5.39). Next D is picked and covers F (3.16 vs 5.00). Result: **p keeps only B and D**.

With alpha = 1.2, E survives: $1.2 \times 5.00 = 6.00 > 5.39$. B is closer to E than p is, but not by a factor of 1.2. Result: **B, D, E**. Larger alpha keeps *more* edges, and the extra ones are long-range.

scenes.caption: Candidates for p with their distance to p. RobustPrune always takes the closest remaining candidate first, so B (1.41) goes first.
alpha = 1: B covers A, C and E because B is closer to each of them than p is (4.00 < 5.10, 3.16 < 4.47, 5.00 < 5.39). Their edges are dropped.
Next D (3.00) is kept and covers F (3.16 < 5.00). With alpha = 1, p ends with just two out-edges: B and D.
alpha = 1.5 keeps four edges (B, D, C, E): only F (via D) and A (via C) are covered. Higher alpha gives a denser graph with more long jumps.

blocks.md: Why keep the long edge to E? Under the alpha rule, every edge that survives guarantees real progress. The paper shows that if every node is pruned with RobustPrune over all other points and $\alpha > 1$, greedy search from any start converges to any base point in a logarithmic number of steps, because the distance to the target shrinks by a factor of about $\alpha$ per hop. With $\alpha = 1$, points on a line give a line graph whose diameter grows like $n$.

blocks.caption: RobustPrune (Algorithm 2 of the DiskANN paper). p_star itself is removed by the filter since its distance to itself is 0.

blocks.md:
**Vamana construction** (Algorithm 3):

1. Start from a random graph where every node has $R$ random out-neighbors. Use the dataset's **medoid** $s$ as the search start.
2. Visit points in random order. For point $p$, run GreedySearch$(s, x_p, 1, L)$ and collect **every node visited**, not just the final $L$ results.
3. Set $p$'s out-edges with RobustPrune on that visited set.
4. Add the reverse edge $p' \to p$ for each new out-neighbor $p'$. If $p'$ now exceeds $R$ edges, RobustPrune $p'$.

Vamana makes **two passes**: first with $\alpha = 1$, then with the user's $\alpha$ (the paper used $\alpha = 2$ in its experiments). The paper reports that the second pass improves the graph, and that running both passes with large $\alpha$ is slower because the first pass then builds a denser graph. Using the visited set as candidates lets Vamana add long-range edges, which is why it does not need HNSW's layer hierarchy.

A common misreading: larger alpha prunes *more*. It is the opposite. The removal test gets harder to pass as alpha grows, so more candidates survive, the average degree rises (up to the cap R), and search paths get shorter. The cost is memory and more distance computations per hop.

blocks.question: In the toy example, alpha = 1.2 kept the edge p to E even though B is closer to E than p is. Which statement explains why that edge is useful?
options: E is p's nearest neighbor
Going through B would bring a search only slightly closer to E (5.00 vs 5.39), so a direct edge gives much faster progress toward points near E
Vamana keeps every edge longer than 5
alpha only affects the build pass, not which edges exist
blocks.explain: Under alpha = 1.2 an edge is dropped only if the detour node is closer to the target by a factor of 1.2 (for E: within 5.39 / 1.2 = 4.49). B is at 5.00, only about 7 percent closer, so the hop through B makes little progress. Keeping long edges where detours are weak is what shrinks the number of hops.

blocks.question: HNSW passes only the final L search results to its pruning step, while Vamana passes every node visited during the search. What does that change?
options: Vamana's graph has no reverse edges
Nothing, the two sets are identical
Vamana sees far-away nodes from early in the path as candidates, so it can create long-range edges without a hierarchy
HNSW becomes slower to build
blocks.explain: Nodes visited early in a greedy walk are far from p. Giving RobustPrune those candidates (together with alpha > 1) lets p keep some long jumps. HNSW gets long jumps from its upper layers instead, which DiskANN avoids because each layer would mean more disk reads.

lessons.title: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking

blocks.md: On disk, DiskANN stores one fixed-size record per node: the node's full-precision vector followed by the ids of its at most $R$ neighbors, padded with zeros if it has fewer. Because every record has the same size, the offset of node $i$ is a multiplication, so no offset table is needed in RAM.

Record size is small. For 128-d float32 vectors and $R = 64$: $128 \times 4 + 64 \times 4 = 768$ bytes. The paper notes that reading a 4 KB-aligned block costs no more than reading 512 bytes, so a node's neighbor list and its full vector arrive in one read.

**BeamSearch** changes one thing in GreedySearch. Instead of expanding the single closest unexpanded candidate, it takes the $W$ closest unexpanded candidates from the list $\mathcal{L}$, fetches all $W$ records in one parallel batch, and scores their neighbors with PQ distances. The paper notes that a few random reads in parallel cost almost the same time as one. $W = 1$ is plain greedy search.

blocks.prompt: Beam width W = 4 instead of W = 1, same list size L = 40. Guess what happens to (a) total SSD reads per query and (b) round trips.
blocks.reveal: Round trips drop sharply (about 3.3x), but total reads go **up** a little, because some of the W nodes fetched in a batch would never have been expanded by a one-at-a-time search. In the simulation below: W = 1 needs 41.5 reads in 41.5 trips, W = 4 needs 44.4 reads in 12.5 trips.

blocks.title: Beam width versus SSD reads (toy simulation, L = 40)

scenes.caption: Average reads (node records fetched) per query. They creep up with W: wider beams fetch some nodes a narrow search would skip.
Average round trips per query. Each trip fetches up to W records in parallel, so trips fall roughly as 1/W.
Recall@10 barely moves (in percent). Beam width is a latency knob, not an accuracy knob; L controls accuracy.

blocks.md: The simulation behind those bars: 5,000 random 32-d Gaussian vectors, Vamana built with $R = 32$, $L = 64$ and passes at $\alpha = 1$ then $1.2$, searched with exact distances from the medoid for 200 queries. Simplified: real DiskANN steers with PQ distances and caches nodes near the start, which removes the first few reads.

blocks.title: Search latency if each round trip costs 200 microseconds

scenes.caption: Model: latency = round trips x 200 us (a stated assumption; the paper says a few hundred microseconds per trip). W = 1 takes 41.5 trips, about 8.3 ms.
W = 2 halves the trips: 22.0 trips, 4.4 ms.
W = 4 and W = 8: 2.5 ms and 1.6 ms. Returns diminish: going from 4 to 8 saves under 1 ms but adds 5 reads per query to the SSD's budget.

blocks.md: The paper explains why you should not just max out W. An SSD reaches its peak IOPS only with deep queues, and then each read takes over a millisecond. DiskANN runs at beam widths like 2, 4 or 8, where the SSD sits at a 30 to 40 percent load and each search thread spends 40 to 50 percent of its time in I/O. It also warns that W of 16 or more wastes compute and bandwidth. The legacy repository's docs say the same: use W = 1 for the highest throughput at a fixed IOPS rating, W = 4 or 8 for best latency (default 2).

blocks.title: Real DiskANN run from the repository docs (W = 2, 100K SIFT)

scenes.caption: Mean 4 KB reads per query grow almost linearly with the search list size L: 8.8 reads at L = 10, 76.6 at L = 100.
Recall@10 in percent for the same runs. Going from L = 20 to L = 100 buys 3.5 points of recall for almost 5x the reads.

blocks.md:
Two more tricks finish the design:

- **Caching**: keep in DRAM the records of all nodes within C = 3 or 4 hops of the start node (or nodes chosen from a known query distribution). The first hops of every query then cost no I/O.
- **Implicit re-ranking**: PQ distances are approximate, so the final order can be wrong. Every record read during search already carries the full vector, so DiskANN re-ranks the visited nodes with exact distances using no extra reads.

For billion-point builds the paper avoids needing 1.1 TB of RAM: k-means splits the data into 40 clusters, each point joins its 2 closest clusters, a Vamana index is built per cluster in memory, and the graphs are merged by taking the union of edges. On SIFT1B this produced a 348 GB index with average degree 92.1, built within 64 GB of RAM. Searched on a 16-core workstation, DiskANN served over 5,000 queries per second at under 3 ms mean latency with 95 percent plus 1-recall@1.

Beam width W trades round trips for wasted reads; search list L trades reads for recall. Tune L for the recall target first, then pick the smallest W that meets the latency target, watching total reads against the SSD's IOPS budget.

blocks.question: A DiskANN service is limited by SSD IOPS at peak traffic, and p99 latency is comfortably under target. Which change is most sensible?
options: Increase W from 4 to 16
Increase L to raise recall
Lower W toward 1 to cut total reads per query
Turn off re-ranking
blocks.explain: Smaller beams waste fewer reads, so each query consumes less of the IOPS budget; latency rises but there is headroom. The repository docs recommend W = 1 for the highest throughput at a fixed IOPS rating. Re-ranking costs no extra reads, so disabling it saves nothing.

blocks.question: Why does DiskANN's re-ranking with full-precision vectors cost no extra SSD reads?
options: Full vectors are cached in RAM
Each node's full vector is stored in the same disk block as its neighbor list, so it arrives with the read the search already made
Re-ranking uses PQ codes only
It reads all candidates in one big sequential read
blocks.explain: The record layout puts the vector next to the adjacency list, inside one 4 KB read. Re-ranking piggybacks on reads the beam search needed anyway. The paper contrasts this with an earlier system that fetched about a hundred candidate vectors at the end, in one burst of random reads.

lessons.title: FreshDiskANN: inserts and deletes without rebuilds

blocks.md: A static index is rebuilt from scratch when data changes. The FreshDiskANN paper (Singh et al., 2021) notes that building a good HNSW index over 100M points takes about 1.5 to 2 hours on a 48-core machine, so keeping a billion-point index six-hourly fresh would need three machines doing nothing but rebuilds. Real systems need inserts and deletes while queries keep running.

Inserts are easy: run GreedySearch for the new point, RobustPrune the visited set to get its out-edges, and add reverse edges (re-pruning any node that exceeds $R$). Deletes are the hard part. The paper tested two natural policies on HNSW, NSG and Vamana, deleting and re-inserting 5 percent of SIFT1M per cycle:

- **Policy A**: drop the deleted node's edges.
- **Policy B**: also connect each in-neighbor to each of the deleted node's out-neighbors, then prune.

Recall kept falling cycle after cycle for all three graphs.

Their diagnosis: aggressive pruning ($\alpha = 1$) makes the graph sparser with every update, so it becomes less navigable. **FreshVamana** applies Policy B with RobustPrune at $\alpha > 1$ (Algorithm 4), which keeps the graph dense. Their experiments show stable recall over 50 cycles of updates, except when $\alpha = 1$.

Toy example on the lesson 2 points. Each node's out-edges come from RobustPrune over all other points with $\alpha = 1.2$ and $R = 3$ (computed by script). Node p has edges to B, D, E, and B has edges to p, C, F. Now B is deleted.

blocks.title: Consolidating a delete around node p

scenes.caption: Before: p points to B, D, E. B points to C and F (and back to p). B is about to be deleted.
Lazy delete: B goes on the DeleteList. Searches may still route through B but never return it. The graph is not touched yet.
Consolidation for p: candidates = p's surviving neighbors {D, E} plus B's neighbors {C, F}. Distances to p: D 3.00, C 4.47, F 5.00, E 5.39.
RobustPrune(alpha 1.2): keep D, which covers F (3.79 <= 5.00); keep C, which covers E (1.2 x 4.12 = 4.95 <= 5.39). p's new edges: D and C. The path p, B, C became p, C.

blocks.md: Deleting eagerly would mean editing every in-neighbor of every deleted node immediately. FreshVamana is lazy: a delete just adds the id to a **DeleteList**. After a non-trivial batch accumulates (the paper suggests 1 to 10 percent of the index), a parallel **delete consolidation** pass runs Algorithm 4 for all affected nodes at once.

The full **FreshDiskANN** system has three parts:

- **LTI** (long-term index): the SSD-resident DiskANN index, with about 25 to 32 bytes of PQ data per point in RAM. Updates do not touch it in real time.
- **TempIndex**: in-memory FreshVamana indexes holding recent inserts. One read-write instance takes inserts; it is periodically frozen into a read-only instance and snapshotted to disk.
- **DeleteList**: ids deleted but still present in some index.

scenes.caption: An insert goes only to the read-write TempIndex in RAM, which runs the FreshVamana insert.
A delete just appends the id to the DeleteList.
A search queries the LTI and every TempIndex, merges results, and filters out ids on the DeleteList.
When the read-only TempIndexes exceed a memory threshold, StreamingMerge folds inserts and deletes into the LTI in the background.

blocks.md:
**StreamingMerge** must use memory proportional to the change, not the index, and keep serving queries. It runs three phases:

1. **Delete**: stream the LTI block by block, run Algorithm 4 on each block, write it back.
2. **Insert**: for each new point, GreedySearch the SSD index and RobustPrune its candidates. Backward edges are not written yet; they go into an in-memory structure $\Delta$.
3. **Patch**: stream the index again, add the $\Delta$ edges to each node, prune if over $R$, write back.

All distance comparisons use the in-memory PQ codes, which is why recall settles slightly below a fresh static build.

The paper gives concrete costs: exactly two sequential passes over the SSD data, about 100 random 4 KB reads per inserted point (a candidate list of 75), and $\Delta$ of size $O(|N| R)$, about 7 GB for 30M inserts at $R = 64$. Note the newer DiskANN3 library in the same repository describes real-time updates with stable recall using logic from FreshDiskANN and IP-DiskANN, without merges.

Do not drop a deleted node's edges and move on. That was Policy A, and recall decayed over update cycles for every graph tested. Repair the neighborhood (connect in-neighbors to the deleted node's out-neighbors) and prune with alpha > 1.

blocks.question: In the toy consolidation, why do B's out-neighbors C and F become candidates for p?
options: Because they are p's nearest points
Because RobustPrune always adds every candidate
Because paths that ran p, B, C or p, B, F must be preserved by giving p a chance to link to them directly
Because C and F were on the DeleteList
blocks.explain: Algorithm 4 adds the deleted node's out-neighbors to the candidate set of each in-neighbor, so navigation through the hole is preserved. RobustPrune then decides which to keep: here C survives and F is covered by D.

blocks.question: A FreshDiskANN deployment sees recall slowly drift down over weeks of merges. The build used alpha = 1 to keep the index small. What is the likely fix?
options: Rebuild with alpha > 1 so update rules keep the graph dense
Increase the DeleteList size
Merge more often
Turn off PQ
blocks.explain: The FreshDiskANN experiments show recall stays stable across update cycles for alpha > 1 but not for alpha = 1, because repeated alpha = 1 pruning makes the graph progressively sparser.

lessons.title: CAGRA: a fixed-degree graph built for GPUs

blocks.md: CAGRA (CUDA ANNS GRAph-based) starts from a different question: what graph shape lets a GPU work efficiently? On an NVIDIA GPU, 32 threads form a **warp** that executes one instruction at a time, warps group into a **CTA** (thread block) that runs on one streaming multiprocessor, and each CTA has small, fast **shared memory**. Irregular work per node wastes threads.

So the CAGRA graph has three deliberate properties:

- **Fixed out-degree $d$**: every node has exactly $d$ neighbors. Uniform work per node avoids load imbalance; on a GPU a small degree would leave threads idle anyway.
- **Directed**, as a consequence of fixed out-degree.
- **No hierarchy**: instead of HNSW's upper layers, search starts from randomly sampled nodes, which a GPU can score in parallel cheaply.

Construction has two stages. First build a k-nearest-neighbor graph with $k = d_{init}$, typically $2d$ or $3d$, using **NN-descent**, which refines approximate neighbor lists by checking neighbors of neighbors (cuVS can also use IVF-PQ), and sort each node's list by distance. A pure kNN graph searches poorly (the paper shows low recall) because neighbor lists are redundant and the graph can split into disconnected pieces. Second, **optimize**: reorder and prune edges, then add reverse edges. The optimization never computes a distance.

**Rank-based reordering.** For an edge X to Y at rank $k$ in X's sorted list, count its **detours**: how many of X's $k$ closer neighbors Z have Y in their own list. Many detours mean Y is easy to reach through other neighbors, so the direct edge is redundant. Keep the $d$ edges with the fewest detours, breaking ties by original rank. This approximates distance by rank, so no distance table is needed.

The toy example below uses 12 grid points: A (1, 0), B (3, 3), C (2, 6), D (2, 5), E (5, 1), F (0, 0), G (3, 6), H (6, 3), I (6, 5), J (5, 0), K (1, 6), L (4, 0), with kNN lists of 8 ($d_{init} = 2d$) pruned to $d = 4$.

blocks.prompt: Node K at (1, 6) has 8 kNN neighbors in order C, D, G, B, I, H, A, F. F is the farthest (6.08). We keep d = 4 edges. Will the edge K to F survive?
blocks.reveal: Yes. F has only **1 detour** (only A lists F), while B, I, H have 3, 4 and 5 detours. The kept edges are C (0), D (1), G (2) and F (1). The farthest kNN neighbor survives because nothing else leads to it; this is the same effect as alpha > 1 in Vamana.

blocks.title: Detour matrix for node K (1 = Z ranks before Y and lists Y)

scenes.caption: Rows are K's neighbors Z, columns are targets Y, both in rank order. A 1 means the edge K to Y can be bypassed via Z. Column sums are the detour counts.
B, I, H have 3, 4, 5 detours: three to five closer neighbors already link to them. These edges are redundant.
F (rank 7, the farthest) has a single detour, via A. Few alternatives mean the edge is valuable, so it is kept despite its length.

blocks.title: Node K: from 8 kNN edges to 4 CAGRA edges

scenes.caption: The kNN list of K sorted by distance (computed from grid coordinates), with each edge's detour count.
Sort by (detours, rank) and keep d = 4: C (0), D (1), F (1), G (2). B, I, H, A are pruned.
Reverse edges: C, D and G keep K in their pruned lists, so K gets reverse candidates C, D, G. The merge takes d/2 = 2 from each side: C, D from the pruned list, then G, then F fills the last slot.

blocks.md: **Reverse edges.** After pruning, CAGRA builds the reversed graph: Y gets an edge back to X for each kept edge X to Y, ordered by that edge's rank in X's pruned list and capped at $d$. Then it merges: take $d/2$ neighbors from the pruned graph and $d/2$ from the reversed graph, filling from the pruned graph if there are too few reverse edges. In the toy graph, node F gains an edge to K this way, linking the bottom-left cluster to the top-left one.

The paper measures two properties. **Strongly connected components**: fewer is better, since a search may not escape a component. **Average 2-hop node count**: how many nodes are reachable in two steps, at most $d + d^2$. Reordering raises the 2-hop count most; reverse edges cut the number of strong components most. Rank-based reordering was up to 1.9x faster than distance-based reordering, which ran out of memory on DEEP-100M, with almost the same recall and throughput.

In the cuVS implementation the detour count is simply the number of closer neighbors whose kNN list contains Y; the paper describes the test with ranks of both hops (max of the two ranks below the edge's rank). Both use rank instead of distance.

blocks.question: Why does CAGRA use rank-based reordering instead of computing distances between neighbors?
options: Ranks give strictly better graphs
Distance-based reordering needs about N x d_init x (d_init - 1) distance computations or an N x d_init distance table, which is slow or runs out of memory at scale
GPUs cannot compute distances
NN-descent does not produce sorted lists
blocks.explain: The paper reports that distance-based reordering was slower and hit out-of-memory on DEEP-100M, while rank-based reordering gave almost the same recall-throughput curve. The rank is a free proxy because NN-descent already sorted each list by distance.

blocks.question: A CAGRA graph built with intermediate degree 128 and graph degree 64 gives too low recall even with large search settings. Per the cuVS tuning guide, what is the build-side knob to try after graph_degree?
options: Lower intermediate_graph_degree
Disable reverse edges
Increase intermediate_graph_degree, giving pruning more choices
Set alpha = 1.2
blocks.explain: cuVS suggests tuning itopk_size first, then graph_degree, then intermediate_graph_degree if graph quality is still too low. A larger kNN graph gives the pruning step more candidates, at a higher build cost. CAGRA has no alpha parameter.

lessons.title: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index

blocks.md: CAGRA search keeps one contiguous buffer per query: an **internal top-M list** (the best M nodes so far, $M \ge k$; cuVS calls it `itopk_size`) followed by a **candidate list** of $p \times d$ slots, where $p$ is the number of parents expanded per iteration (`search_width`, default 1) and $d$ the graph degree. Each entry is a node id and its distance to the query.

One iteration has three steps:

1. **Top-M update**: keep the M smallest distances from the whole buffer (top list plus candidates).
2. **Graph traversal**: pick the best $p$ nodes in the top-M list that have not been parents yet, and copy all their neighbor ids into the candidate list.
3. **Distance calculation**: compute distances only for nodes seen for the first time; a visited-node hash table filters the rest.

The search stops when the top-M ids stop changing, and returns the first $k$.
Here it runs on the toy CAGRA graph from lesson 5 (12 points, $d = 4$), with $M = 4$, $p = 1$, query at (0, 6). Distances are Euclidean on the grid and were computed by script.

blocks.title: CAGRA search buffer, iteration by iteration

scenes.caption: Step 0: sample p x d = 4 random nodes (E, H, A, L) and compute their distances to the query at (0, 6). Step 1 copies the best M = 4 into the top-M list. Parent: A.
Step 2 copies parent A's 4 neighbors into the candidate list. Step 3 scores only first-time nodes: L was already scored, so it is skipped. B (4.24) jumps to the top. Next parent: B.
B's neighbors are D, E, A, F; only D is new (2.24). Three of four slots were wasted on known nodes, which the hash table detects cheaply. Next parent: D.
D's neighbors C, G, B, K bring three new nodes, including K at 1.00, the true nearest neighbor. Next parent: K.
K's neighbors C, D, G, F are all known, so the top-M list is unchanged: the search has converged. Return the top k entries, here K (1.00) and C (2.00).

blocks.md:
GPU details that make this fast, from the paper:

- **Warp splitting**: one distance is computed by a *team* of 4, 8, 16 or 32 threads (the cuVS `team_size`). A 96-d float vector is 3072 bits, less than the 4096 bits a full warp loads with 128-bit loads, so one distance per warp would leave a quarter of the warp idle; teams of 8 let one warp compute four distances at once.
- **Sorting**: top-M merges use a warp-level bitonic sort when the candidate buffer has at most 512 entries, and a radix-based sort across the CTA above that.
- **Forgettable hash table**: in single-CTA mode the visited table lives in shared memory (typically 4 KB or less per query) and is periodically reset, keeping only the current top-M. Recomputing a few distances is cheaper than a big table.
- **Parent flag**: whether a node has been a parent is stored in the top bit of its id, which limits a 32-bit index to $2^{31} - 1$ nodes.

**Single-CTA vs multi-CTA.** Single-CTA maps one query to one thread block, good for large batches (100 and up). For small batches that would leave most of the GPU idle, multi-CTA runs one query on several CTAs that each expand one parent and share a hash table in device memory. The paper uses multi-CTA when the batch is smaller than the number of SMs or when M exceeds 512. In cuVS, `algo = AUTO` makes this choice.

blocks.title: CAGRA speedups reported in the paper (upper end of each range)

scenes.caption: Graph build: 2.2 to 27x faster than HNSW. Large-batch search at 90 to 95 percent recall: 33 to 77x HNSW and 3.8 to 8.8x other GPU methods.
Lower ends of the same ranges. Single-query search: 3.4 to 53x faster than HNSW at 95 percent recall, thanks to multi-CTA. Ranges depend on dataset and hardware (A100 vs a 64-core EPYC).

# build on the GPU (defaults: intermediate_graph_degree=128, graph_degree=64)
index = cagra.build(cagra.IndexParams(graph_degree=64), dataset)

# search on the GPU: itopk_size is the main recall knob (default 64)
distances, neighbors = cagra.search(
    cagra.SearchParams(itopk_size=128), index, queries, 10)

# or convert to HNSW and serve on CPUs
hnsw_index = hnsw.from_cagra(hnsw.IndexParams(hierarchy="gpu"), index)

blocks.md: **CAGRA to HNSW.** cuVS can convert a CAGRA graph into an hnswlib-format HNSW index, so GPUs do the expensive build and CPUs serve queries. The `hierarchy` option chooses a base-layer-only index (`NONE`) or a full index with upper layers built on the CPU or GPU. The guide also advises not keeping the dataset attached to the CAGRA index when converting right after build (`attach_dataset_on_build = False` in C++).

Choosing: **DiskANN** when the data is far larger than RAM and an SSD is acceptable (a few ms per query at high recall on one machine). **CAGRA** when vectors fit in GPU memory and you need high throughput or fast builds; IVF-PQ initial graph builds can run in batches on datasets larger than GPU memory. **CAGRA then HNSW** when you build on GPUs but serve on CPUs.

blocks.question: In the toy search, the query's true nearest neighbor K was not in the random start sample. How did the search reach it?
options: The hash table stored K's distance in advance
Each iteration expanded the best non-parent node (A, then B, then D), and D's neighbor list contained K
Multi-CTA mode searched all nodes
K was added by the reverse-edge step during search
blocks.explain: Search moves through parents: A gave B, B gave D, and D's out-edges include K. The top-M list stopped changing after K was expanded, so the search ended. Reverse edges matter at build time, not search time.

blocks.question: A recommendation service sends one query at a time to a GPU CAGRA index, and the GPU is mostly idle. Which setting addresses this?
options: Multi-CTA search, which spreads one query across several thread blocks
A larger team_size
A smaller graph_degree
Single-CTA with a persistent kernel
blocks.explain: Single-CTA maps a query to one block, so a batch of 1 uses a sliver of the GPU. Multi-CTA assigns several CTAs to one query, each expanding a parent, which the paper designed for batch sizes of about 1 to 100. cuVS AUTO selects it for small batches.
